scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a policy response that grants the value of honest guidance, then argues that actively discouraging students would do more harm than good; two developed examples weighing consequences, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Schools naturally want their students to succeed and to avoid wasted effort.
One proposed policy is that educational institutions should discourage students from studying fields in which they are unlikely to succeed.
I agree that schools should give honest guidance, but I believe actively discouraging students would do more harm than good.
First, the policy is built on a fair concern for students' futures.
Honest advice can save a student from years of struggle and heavy debt in a hopeless direction.
For example, a counsellor who gently warns a weak maths student about a demanding engineering course may spare her real disappointment.
This shows that realistic guidance can be a genuine kindness.
Institutions also have limited places and resources, which should not be wasted carelessly.
Pointing students toward fields that suit them can help them flourish.
To this extent, the policy contains a sensible idea.
Second, however, actively dissuading students can crush ambition and prove badly mistaken.
Teachers often cannot predict who will succeed, because effort and passion can overcome early weakness.
Consider the many famous scientists and writers who were once judged hopeless by their own teachers.
Discouraging such students would have robbed the world of their later achievements.
A policy of this kind could also push young people away from the very dreams that motivate them.
It risks turning schools into gatekeepers that decide futures far too early.
Guidance should open doors, not close them before a student has truly tried.
In conclusion, schools should offer students honest and realistic advice about their chances.
But a policy of actively discouraging them would stifle ambition and often turn out to be wrong.
The better path is to inform and support students while leaving the final choice in their hands.
